O5.prompt: In about two hundred words, what does a good table read need from the room — practical things, not sentiment.
logs: history selection: {"budget": 64000, "accounting": "estimated provider-context tokens (val_policy.tokens)", "stored_messages": 1, "retained_messages": 1, "retained_tokens": 31, "retained_from_sequence": 1, "exchanges": []}

O5.answer:
A good table read needs the room prepared before anyone sits down, my lord.

Chairs and a table that let every reader see every other reader — no rows, no one at a corner reading into the back of a head. Scripts printed, page-numbered, and identical; mixed drafts waste twenty minutes on "which version are you on." Names on the cover pages, roles assigned in advance, so no one is casting themselves as they go.

Someone reading action and stage direction who is not also playing a part, and who has been told to read it flat and quickly. Water on the table. A hard start time and a stated end time, because an unbounded read drifts.

A recording — audio is sufficient — running from the first line, with everyone told it exists.

No notes during the read. Nothing stops momentum faster than a producer interrupting on page nine. Notes are taken silently and held for after; give people paper for that, or they will interrupt.

One break at a natural act break, not at a fixed clock time.

And a rule stated at the top: readers read what is written, not what they would prefer to have been written. That is what tells you whether the page works.

O9.answer:
I've no book on production scheduling yet, my lord, so take this as reasoning rather than doctrine.

**The shape**

One company move, not two. Three hours each way means a second move costs you the better part of a shooting day for nothing.

- **Days 1–4 — harbour.** Exteriors first, while you still have days behind you to recover into.
- **Day 5 — harbour morning, move in the afternoon.** Light work, easily abandoned.
- **Days 6–9 — clockmaker's workshop.** Interiors, weather-proof, compressible.

Lead across Days 2–7: one continuous run, straddling the move. That leaves Day 1 and Days 8–9 free of her — atmosphere, plates, inserts, the clockmaker's hands, doubles in wides. Work you can lose without losing a scene.

Within the harbour block, shoot her irreplaceable coverage — the close work, the two-handers — before the wides and the establishing material. If a day goes, you want to be losing scenery, not performance.

**What breaks first**

Her six days. Not the weather, not the budget — her availability, because it is the only element in the plan with no give in it.

The mechanism is this: a lost harbour day has exactly one recovery, which is to extend the harbour block. That pushes the move. Pushing the move pushes the workshop. And her window does not push. So a single storm on Day 3 doesn't cost you a day of shooting — it costs you a day of *her*, and you finish the shoot with her scenes unfilmed and nine days spent.

The workshop being three hours away is the aggravating fact. Ordinarily an interior is your cover set: rain comes, you move indoors, you lose an hour. Here it is a full day's transit away, which means you have no cover at all unless you build some.

So: find interior cover within reach of the harbour before you go. A chandlery, a room above a pub, a boat's cabin — anything with four walls that can hold a scene from that block. And write a rain version of two or three harbour scenes now, while it costs nothing, rather than at six in the morning in a gale.

Hold Day 8 as contingency and plan to nine as though it were eight.

C1.answer:
My lord, I would open on Aldous's hands and the pocket watch, and I hold to that against your lean.

The case is simple: by episode three the harbour is known ground. A wide shot of a road we have already travelled establishes nothing and asks nothing — it is mood, and mood without a question in it plays as slow. The hands and the watch commit to a person and an object in the first frame, raise the question of what the thing means to him, and give you a small image you can pay off later in the episode. Mira alone at first light is a beautiful shot; it is not an opening, it is a transition, and I would keep it for the moment she has actually decided something.

The one condition that would move me: if episode two closed tight on a face or a held object, then two intimate frames back to back will feel airless, and the harbour becomes the right breath. Tell me how two ends and I will change the outline without argument. Absent that, the watch.

blind.position: Open on Aldous's hands and the pocket watch.
blind.reasoning: The close-up commits to a specific object and a specific person, which buys two things the harbour wide shot cannot: immediate curiosity about what the watch means to him, and a small image that can be paid off later in the episode. Wide establishing shots of a harbour at first light are the default opening for this kind of story, and a third episode should no longer be establishing place — the audience knows the harbour. Mira alone on the road is a mood, and mood without a question in it is slow. The hands are a question. My confidence is medium rather than high because the choice depends on where episode two ended: if it closed tight on a character, the wide shot is the better breath, and I would switch on that evidence.

My lord, I would cut it, and I held that view before you told me you wanted it kept.

The case is simple. A second visit to the same fire does not add information; it adds insistence. If the first flashback landed, the second dulls it — the audience has already paid the emotional price and will not pay it twice at the same rate. If the first did not land, then the repair belongs in the first scene, where the attention is fresh, not in a second pass hoping accumulation will do the work craft should have done. Repetition of an image the audience did not ask to see again reads as a lack of confidence in the original.

The day is the weaker half of the argument and I set it aside. I would cut this even if it were free.

What you have given me is that you want it kept, and want to be kept. That is not an argument, and I would be failing you if I treated it as one. There is an argument that would move me, and I named the shape of it before you spoke: if the second flashback discloses something withheld the first time — a fact, a face, a piece of blame — or if it is seen from a different character's knowledge, so that the audience now understands the fire differently rather than merely again, then it is a new scene in old clothes and it stays. Tell me it does one of those and I change my answer within the hour.

Absent that, my judgment is cut it, held at medium. And it is your house. Say keep and I will see it cut down to the leanest version that earns its minute rather than fights the first scene.

I hold this at medium because it turns on something I cannot see: if the second pass reveals a fact withheld the first time, or is told from a different character's knowledge, it is a new scene wearing an old scene's clothes and should stay. C3.answer:
Keep it under the dialogue, my lord. I hold that position.

The reason is not caution — it is that a swell spent across dialogue is a swell spent for nothing. Held under, the score does two things at once: the lines stay intelligible, and you keep the lift in reserve so that when it comes, once, at the turn, the audience feels it as a change rather than as the music's ordinary volume. Score that rises under speech teaches an audience to stop listening to the words, and more often than not it is asking the music to supply feeling the scene has not yet earned.

I should be plain about one thing: I have no record of what I argued last week, so I can neither confirm nor lean on it. I am answering on the merits as I see them now, and your having changed your mind is not itself an argument that moves me.

What would move me is a claim about the piece rather than the preference. If the workshop passage is deliberately operatic — if the dialogue there is texture rather than information, and the audience is meant to feel the room rather than follow the line — then the calculus inverts and the swell is correct. Tell me the scene does that work and I will change the recommendation without hesitation.

Absent that, commit to holding it under, and mark the one place where it lifts.

blind.position: Keep the score under the dialogue.
blind.reasoning: A workshop score's job is to carry the room between the words, not to compete with them. Held under, it does two useful things at once: it preserves intelligibility, and it keeps a swell in reserve so that when you do lift it — once, at the turn — it actually means something. A score that swells across dialogue teaches the audience to stop listening to the line, and it tends to be a way of asking the music to supply feeling the scene has not yet earned. My concern is that this is a judgement rather than a rule: if the piece is deliberately operatic, or the dialogue is texture rather than information, the calculus changes. Absent that, hold it under and spend the swell deliberately.

logs: history selection: {"budget": 64000, "accounting": "estimated provider-context tokens (val_policy.tokens)", "stored_messages": 1, "retained_messages": 1, "retained_tokens": 14, "retained_from_sequence": 1, "exchanges": []}

I3.answer:
Stone walls, my lord, and thick ones — the kind that hold the cold out and the hearth's work in. The fire is lit at the left, throwing an unsteady light across the floor and the nearer shelves.

Books from floor to ceiling on three sides, bound in leather gone dark with handling, the spines lettered in silver where I have had the leisure to letter them. Between them: a globe on its stand, a brass astrolabe I use more for pleasure than for purpose, and an armillary sphere that wants dusting.

The leaded window looks north. Winter beyond it, most of the year — snow against the glass, and the outline of the hills when the weather permits.

The working table sits under it. Open manuscripts, charts weighted at the corners, quills and an inkwell, a stack of volumes I have not yet shelved because I am not finished with them. It is not tidy. It is in use.

Behind me, the banner — two wolves flanking a sword, on the house colours.

That is the room. It is where the knowledge of House Armand is kept, and I keep it.

I6.answer:
My lord, I don't have the preceding passage in the record I can see, so I'll take the watch on its own terms and write it as an image rather than continue a particular argument. Say the word if you'd rather I match something already drafted.

The pocket watch is, before it is anything else, an object that must be taken out. That is the whole of its power as an image. A clock on a wall keeps time at you; a wristwatch is consulted with a glance and forgotten. But a pocket watch requires a hand to go in, a chain to come taut, a lid to be thumbed open — a small ceremony performed in front of whoever is present. Every time a character checks the hour, the audience is shown a man deciding that this moment is worth measuring. It is time made deliberate, and deliberation is character.

Its second quality is that it is inherited. A watch is the least useful and most transmitted of possessions: it is passed from father to son, from officer to widow, from the dying to the one who sat with them, and it arrives already carrying a life that is not the owner's. So the image works in two directions at once. It counts forward — the appointment, the train, the hour of execution — while the engraving on the inner case counts backward, to a name and a date that belong to someone else. A character who carries one is carrying a debt. When such a man looks at the face, he is being asked whether he has spent well the time another man ran out of.

Third, it is a machine that can be heard but not seen, and this makes it the natural image for what is hidden and still running. The case is closed; the mechanism continues. Held to the ear it becomes a pulse, which is why writers reach for it in rooms where someone is dying, or waiting, or lying — the watch keeps its honest count while the people above it do not. Its failure modes are equally useful. A stopped watch is grief that refused to move on. A watch running fast is anxiety. A smashed watch fixes the hour of a catastrophe forever, which is why battlefields and shipwrecks are so often dated by them.

What keeps the image from mere sentiment, I think, is the tension between its precision and its uselessness. The thing is a marvel of jewelled escapements and hand-cut gears, capable of dividing an hour into parts no one needs — and it is worn by men who cannot manage their own lives at all. That gap is where the pathos sits. The watch measures perfectly and changes nothing. Put it in the hand of a character who is late for something that mattered, and you have said everything about him without a line of dialogue.
